page-open-source-meta-description: Free and open source software puts control back with the people who use it. Learn what open source means, what it makes possible, and why Ethereum is built in the open.
page-open-source-hero-description-1: So much of daily life depends on software: the phone in your pocket, the services in your home, the apps you use every day. When a single platform controls those tools, it gains unhealthy power and dictates how you're allowed to use them.
page-open-source-hero-description-2: Free and open source software puts that power back where it belongs: with the user, ensuring technology serves you and your community over corporate interests.
page-open-source-summary-item-1: Open source means that the underlying technology is publicly available for anyone to use, copy, improve, or build on.
page-open-source-summary-item-2: Modern digital life trades your sovereignty for convenience. Free and open source software is the practical path back: giving you privacy and protection from monetary exploitation.
page-open-source-summary-item-3: You don't need to read code to benefit. Openness means independent experts can check what software really does, and their scrutiny protects everyone.
page-open-source-summary-item-4: Ethereum is built in the open: its specifications, client software, and even this website can be inspected and improved by anyone.
page-open-source-ownership-title: When the things you buy stop being yours
page-open-source-ownership-description-1: Most of your digital life is operated by a handful of big companies. You may not be able to see how your data is used, why your feed algorithm changes, and have no recourse when a feature you rely on disappears. In exchange, everything is convenient.
page-open-source-ownership-description-3: In 2009, Amazon reached into customers' Kindles and <link1>remotely deleted books people had bought and paid for</link1>. As recently as 2024, Spotify discontinued its Car Thing device and <link2>remotely disabled units that customers had purchased</link2>.
page-open-source-ownership-description-4: These cases show the risk of closed software: when a product depends on code and servers controlled by one vendor, that vendor can decide whether the product continues to work.
page-open-source-ownership-description-5: Open source changes the balance. When the code behind a product is public and its license grants meaningful rights, people can inspect it, run it, repair it, adapt it, and continue it independently. It is the same argument the right-to-repair movement makes about hardware, applied to the software inside it.
page-open-source-definition-title: What does "free and open source" mean?
page-open-source-definition-description-: Free/libre and open source software (FLOSS, also written FOSS) is software whose source code, the instructions that make it work, is public for anyone to run, study, share, and improve. Think of a dish that comes with its full recipe: you can check the ingredients, cook it yourself, pass it on, or make it better. Closed software keeps the recipe and ingredients secret, so one company decides what goes in, who may eat, and whether you ever find out.
"Free" here means freedom, not price. A program can cost money and still be free software; a no-cost app can still be closed and restrictive.

The idea is simple: if a company controls the code, the company controls the user. Free software flips that. It guarantees, legally and permanently, that the software answers to you. In plain language, it grants four freedoms:
page-open-source-freedom-run-description: Run the program as you wish, for any purpose, on your own terms.
page-open-source-freedom-study-descripti: Examine the source code to see exactly how the program works, then change it to suit your own needs.
page-open-source-freedom-share-descripti: Give other people exact copies of the program, so they can use it too.
page-open-source-freedom-distribute-desc: Release your modified version, so the wider community benefits from your changes.
page-open-source-definition-description-: Examples of open source software include Linux, the kernel inside every Android phone and most servers, Firefox, VLC, LibreOffice, and Signal, whose encryption protocol also secures WhatsApp messages. Chances are you have used open source software today without noticing.
page-open-source-traditions-question: So is it "free software" or "open source"?
page-open-source-traditions-answer-1: "Free software" and "open source" come from related traditions. Free software emphasizes users' rights and freedom. Open source often emphasizes practical benefits such as collaboration, reliability, and better software. In practice, both describe software whose license grants people real rights to use, study, modify, and share it.
page-open-source-traditions-answer-2: This page uses the terms together, as FLOSS, because the distinction rarely changes what you can do with the software in front of you.
page-open-source-possible-title: What does open source make possible?
page-open-source-possible-description: Free software is a neutral, universally accessible tool for controlling your own digital life. It belongs to no political ideology or movement; it works the same for everyone who runs it.
page-open-source-benefit-trust-descripti: Open code lets independent people inspect how software works. Security, privacy, and accessibility claims can be tested rather than accepted on faith.
page-open-source-benefit-leave-descripti: Open software and open formats can make it easier to move your data and avoid being locked into one vendor. The details matter: a product should also provide practical export and migration options.
page-open-source-benefit-outlives-descri: When a company shuts down or moves on, open code lets anyone keep the lights on.
page-open-source-security-question: Isn't open source less secure if anyone can read the code?
page-open-source-security-answer-1: It is a fair question, and the answer is not a flat no. Publishing code does let attackers study it. But it lets everyone else study it too, and secrecy has a poor record as a defense: closed software has the same flaws, found later, disclosed on the vendor's schedule, and fixed when it suits them.
page-open-source-security-answer-2: The honest version is that openness is necessary but not sufficient. Serious bugs have sat unnoticed in widely used open projects for years, usually because critical infrastructure was being maintained by one or two unpaid people. What openness guarantees is that anyone can look and anyone can fix it; whether enough people do depends on how well the project is funded and staffed. That is worth checking before you depend on something, and it is an easy thing to ask about.
page-open-source-collaboration-descripti: Open source allows people to learn from one another's work, report bugs, translate interfaces, write documentation, improve accessibility, and build tools for needs a commercial roadmap might overlook.
page-open-source-repair-description: A device usually dies when its software does: the updates stop, the server goes dark, the app is pulled, and working hardware becomes waste. The right-to-repair movement fights this in law, pushing back on locked firmware, paired parts, and rules that make fixing your own property a violation. Open source is the software half of the same fight. When the code can be read, patched, and rebuilt by whoever owns the device, a product can outlast its maker's interest in selling you the next one.
page-open-source-speech-description: Publishing code is speech, and it has had to be defended as such: the right to publish encryption software was won in court in the 1990s, which is why strong encryption is available to ordinary people today. The reverse holds too. When one company controls a tool, it decides what can be said, read, or built with it, and a policy change can silence work that was fine the day before. Two of the four freedoms, sharing copies and publishing your changes, are a right to republish, and software that anyone may copy cannot be quietly switched off.
page-open-source-fork-description: If maintainers take a project in a bad direction, the community can copy the code and continue on its own path. LibreOffice, Jenkins, and OpenTofu all exist because communities exercised this right when corporate owners changed course. Forks are the safeguard against capture.
page-open-source-switch-title: How to switch to open source apps
page-open-source-switch-description-1: You do not need to replace everything at once. Start with one tool you use often and choose the outcome that matters most to you: better privacy, fewer subscriptions, local control, data portability, or the ability to contribute.
page-open-source-switch-description-2: Consider tradeoffs honestly. FLOSS and privacy-protecting software sometimes trades convenience for control: anti-tracking protection may occasionally break heavily scripted websites, untracked search may lack hyper-localized predictions, and maps that refuse to follow you may lack real-time traffic.
page-open-source-app-bitwarden-descripti: A password manager that syncs across all your devices
page-open-source-app-brave-description: A familiar browser that blocks trackers by default
page-open-source-app-firefox-description: An independent browser built by a non-profit, not based on Chromium
page-open-source-app-signal-description: A mainstream chat app with gold-standard encryption
page-open-source-app-cryptomator-descrip: Encrypts your files before they reach the cloud
page-open-source-app-thunderbird-descrip: A long-standing desktop mail client that works with any provider
page-open-source-app-organic-maps-descri: Offline navigation on OpenStreetMap data, with no location tracking
page-open-source-app-vlc-description: Plays almost any audio or video file, with no ads or accounts
page-open-source-app-grapheneos-descript: A hardened Android build for Pixel phones, with no Google services
page-open-source-app-debian-description: A community-run Linux distribution that many others are built on
page-open-source-app-ubuntu-description: A beginner-friendly Linux desktop with long-term support releases
page-open-source-app-home-assistant-desc: Runs your smart home locally, without the vendor's cloud
page-open-source-app-immich-description: A self-hosted photo and video library on hardware you own
page-open-source-app-logseq-description: Notes and journals stored as plain files on your device
page-open-source-app-libreoffice-descrip: Documents, spreadsheets, and slides that open the files you already have
page-open-source-app-localsend-descripti: Sends files between devices over your own network
page-open-source-app-obs-description: Records and streams your screen, with no watermarks or subscriptions
page-open-source-app-blender-description: A full 3D suite, from modeling and animation to video editing
page-open-source-app-inkscape-descriptio: Vector drawing for logos, icons, and illustration
page-open-source-app-gimp-description: A long-standing image editor for photo retouching and design work
page-open-source-alternativeto-descripti: Discover powerful open-source alternatives to popular software.
page-open-source-resources-catalogs: <switching>Switching.software</switching> and <privacyguides>Privacy Guides</privacyguides>: more catalogs of open replacements for everyday software.
page-open-source-resources-degoogled: De-Googled ecosystems: <grapheneos>GrapheneOS</grapheneos>, <eos>/e/OS</eos>, <lineageos>LineageOS</lineageos>, <fdroid>F-Droid</fdroid>; open hardware from <framework>Framework</framework>, <pine64>Pine64</pine64>, and <mnt>MNT Reform</mnt>.
page-open-source-ai-intro: AI cuts both ways here. The assistants most people use are proprietary services running on someone else's computer. But they are also, right now, one of the best tools available for getting started with open source software, and there are open models you can run yourself that never phone home at all.
page-open-source-ai-assist-title: Let AI lower the barrier to entry
page-open-source-ai-assist-description-1: The hard part of switching is rarely the software itself. It is everything around it: knowing what exists, working out whether it is any good, getting it installed, and figuring out what to do when something breaks. Big companies spend a lot of money smoothing that path. Volunteer projects usually cannot, so the friction lands on you.
page-open-source-ai-assist-description-2: An AI assistant removes most of that friction, and you do not need to be technical to use one. Describe what you want in plain words, then keep asking follow-up questions until the answer makes sense. It never gets impatient.
page-open-source-ai-superpower-title: You don't have to read the code yourself
page-open-source-ai-superpower-descripti: Open source software can be inspected by anyone, and plenty of people do. But you don't need a developer's skill set to check the one thing that worries you. Describe the concern in plain words and an assistant will read the code and answer in plain words. The openness was always there, and assistants put it within reach.
page-open-source-ai-prompts-lead: Things worth asking. Copy any of these and fill in the blanks:
page-open-source-ai-prompt-alternatives-: What are the open source alternatives to [app] for [my device], and what would I give up by switching?
Open projects rarely have marketing budgets, so the good ones are hard to find.
page-open-source-ai-prompt-reputation-te: Who makes [app]? How is it funded, is it still actively maintained, and has it ever had security problems?
page-open-source-ai-prompt-reputation-de: A background check on a project you would otherwise trust blind.
page-open-source-ai-prompt-policy-text: Find [app]'s privacy policy and license, and tell me in plain English what data leaves my device.
page-open-source-ai-prompt-policy-descri: Fine print is written to be skimmed past. An assistant reads all of it.
page-open-source-ai-prompt-permissions-t: [App] is asking for permission to access my contacts. Check the project's source code and tell me what it actually does with them.
page-open-source-ai-prompt-permissions-d: It can go read the project's own code and tell you what that permission is really for.
page-open-source-ai-prompt-install-text: Walk me through installing [app] on [my system], one step at a time, and tell me what each step does.
page-open-source-ai-prompt-install-descr: Answers for your exact machine, instead of docs written for a generic one.
page-open-source-ai-prompt-error-text: I tried this and got this error. What does it mean, and what should I try next?
page-open-source-ai-prompt-error-descrip: The step where most people give up, when there is no support line to call.
page-open-source-ai-tip-description: Most assistants let you save standing preferences, variously called custom instructions, memory, or a project configuration file. Add something like "always prefer free and open source options, and tell me the license" and every future conversation starts from there. You stop having to ask, and open alternatives simply show up in the answers by default.
page-open-source-ai-assist-caveats: Two habits are worth keeping. Assistants are sometimes confidently wrong, so treat what you get as a well-informed starting point: check download links and install commands against the project's own website before running them, and remember that a code explanation is a second pair of eyes, not a security audit. And if you are using a hosted assistant, everything you type into it goes to that company's servers, which is a good reason to read on.
page-open-source-local-ai-title: Running AI on your own computer
page-open-source-local-ai-description-1: Most chat assistants are services. Your prompt leaves your device, the company sets the rules, and access can be changed, priced, or discontinued at any time. It does not have to work that way.
page-open-source-local-ai-description-2: Models with published weights can be downloaded and run on hardware you already own. No account. No API key. No subscription. Nothing sent anywhere, so you can unplug the network and keep working. And once the file is on your disk, it is yours: no one can deprecate it, silently change it, or take it away. A model you download today will still answer questions on that machine in ten years.
page-open-source-local-ai-item-jan: Jan: a desktop app with a visual model browser and no command line at any point. Fully open source, built around offline use, with no mandatory cloud account.
page-open-source-local-ai-item-ollama: Ollama: its desktop app downloads and chats with models entirely from the interface, and it doubles as the engine behind a large ecosystem of other tools.
page-open-source-local-ai-item-lm-studio: LM Studio: a polished first install experience, with a model browser that flags what your hardware can handle. The app itself is closed source, though the models it runs are not.
page-open-source-local-ai-description-4: Everything runs on hardware you already own. As a rough guide, multiply a model's size in billions of parameters by 0.6 to estimate how many gigabytes of memory it wants, so an 8-billion-parameter model needs around 5 GB free. A model that size is slower and less capable than a large hosted one, but can summarize, draft, and answer everyday questions perfectly well, including every question in the section above, with nothing leaving your machine.
page-open-source-local-ai-note-title: What does it mean for a model to be "open"?
page-open-source-local-ai-note-descripti: Most models described as open publish their weights but not their training data or the code that produced them. You can run and adapt them; you cannot fully study or rebuild them. By the definitions set out on this page, that is closer to source-available than to free software.

It is still a large improvement on the closed alternative. An open-weight model you have downloaded runs without permission, cannot be revoked, keeps working when the company behind it changes direction or disappears, and can be independently tested by anyone who wants to check its behavior. Those are the same benefits, freedom to leave and software that outlives its maker, that the rest of this page is about. The Open Source Initiative's Open Source AI Definition sets out what full openness would require, and a handful of models such as AI2's OLMo and EleutherAI's Pythia already meet it.
page-open-source-movement-description: Long before Ethereum existed, people were making these arguments and winning them. They wrote the licenses described on this page, won the court cases that made publishing code lawful, and built the tools millions rely on to speak and read unwatched. Privacy, ownership, repair, freedom of speech, the right to read: Ethereum holds the same commitments because it grew out of the same tradition, and the organizations below are where much of that ground is still defended, case by case and tool by tool. Much of what this page describes exists because of them. They are independent of Ethereum and set their own priorities, and all of them are worth supporting.
page-open-source-org-fsf-description: Maintains the free software definition and the GNU project
page-open-source-org-eff-description: Defends digital civil liberties in the courts and in public policy
page-open-source-org-osi-description: Stewards the open source definition and the list of approved licenses
page-open-source-org-tor-description: Builds open anonymity and anti-censorship tools
page-open-source-org-fight-for-the-futur: Campaigns for an open internet and against mass surveillance
page-open-source-org-internet-archive-de: Preserves the web and defends the right to read, lend, and archive online
page-open-source-movement-wider-descript: The same value shows up well beyond software. Some of the most useful knowledge ever put online is free to anyone with a connection, because the people who built it chose to keep it that way: a peer-reviewed university textbook, course material from world-class universities, an encyclopedia in hundreds of languages, a map of the entire planet, research that would otherwise sit behind a paywall. For someone with no institutional access and nothing to spend, that is the difference between being able to learn something and not. It is the same instinct that keeps software open, turned on knowledge itself.
page-open-source-resources-data: Open science: <doaj>DOAJ</doaj> for open access journals, <arxiv>arXiv</arxiv> for preprints, and <zenodo>Zenodo</zenodo> for research data and code.
page-open-source-resources-culture: Open culture: <cc>Creative Commons</cc>, the public domain, <wikipedia>Wikipedia</wikipedia>, <osm>OpenStreetMap</osm>.
page-open-source-ethereum-description-1: Ethereum is a public network built through open specifications and independently developed software. No single company owns the protocol or has exclusive control over how people access it. Anyone can inspect the code, review proposed changes, run software that connects to the network, or build applications that use the protocol.
page-open-source-ethereum-item-1: The network's rules are implemented by multiple independent teams, so no single company controls what it does.
page-open-source-ethereum-item-2: Anyone can run a node and independently verify the network.
page-open-source-ethereum-item-3: Researchers and developers discuss protocol changes openly.
page-open-source-ethereum-item-4: Contributors can improve code, documentation, translations, education, tooling, and community resources.
page-open-source-ethereum-description-2: A different future is possible, one where openness is built in and the things you rely on keep working for you.
page-open-source-ethereum-description-3: Ethereum's openness does not mean every application built on it is open source, safe, or trustworthy. You should still evaluate the software, contracts, teams, and risks involved. But the protocol itself is designed so that its foundations can be inspected and improved in public.
page-open-source-comparison-title: Proprietary, open source, and free software: what's the difference?
page-open-source-comparison-description: "Open" gets used loosely, and the differences matter. Four families cover almost everything you will meet:
page-open-source-comparison-proprietary-: You can use the software only under the vendor's terms. You generally cannot inspect, modify, or redistribute it.
No license to the source at all
page-open-source-comparison-source-avail: You can read the code. Commercial use, modification, or redistribution are restricted. Not open source.
BUSL 1.1, SSPL, many "open core" licenses. Not OSI-approved.
Terraform, which moved from the open MPL 2.0 to BUSL 1.1 in August 2023. That change is why the community forked OpenTofu.
page-open-source-comparison-permissive-r: You can generally use, study, modify, and share the software, including in commercial products, subject to license conditions.
page-open-source-comparison-permissive-e: Lighthouse, Reth, Besu, Teku (Apache 2.0); Nimbus (Apache 2.0 / MIT); this website (MIT)
page-open-source-comparison-copyleft-rig: You can use, study, modify, and share the software. If you distribute modified versions, the license may require you to pass on the same freedoms.
page-open-source-comparison-copyleft-exa: Linux (GPL-2.0); Ethereum clients: go-ethereum (GPL-3.0 for the binary, LGPL-3.0 for its libraries); Prysm, Nethermind, Grandine, Solidity (GPL-3.0)
page-open-source-copyleft-title: Ethereum runs on copyleft, not just on the word "open"
page-open-source-copyleft-description-1: Plenty of projects call themselves open. What matters is the license file, so here is ours.
page-open-source-copyleft-description-2: Ethereum's most critical infrastructure ships under the Free Software Foundation's own copyleft licenses: go-ethereum is GPL-3.0 with LGPL-3.0 libraries, and Prysm, Nethermind, Grandine, and the Solidity compiler are GPL-3.0, with Erigon under LGPL-3.0. Other clients take the permissive route: Lighthouse, Reth, Besu, and Teku are Apache 2.0. This website is MIT, and every change to this page is publicly visible.
page-open-source-copyleft-contribute: That includes this page: you can read its <source>source</source>, <issues>suggest a change</issues>, or help <translation>translate it</translation>.
page-open-source-copyleft-description-3: Client diversity is itself an application of the right to fork. No single implementation controls the network, and any of them can be replaced by something better without asking permission.
